deep.reconstruction:
Dated 5.1.84. Grothendieck moves from pseudoline arrangements to a more general setting. He takes a compact surface X with a topological graph X_1 ⊂ X that decomposes X into cells. The main case he has in mind is when every vertex of X_1 has even order. The model example is (X, X_1) = a system of pseudolines in a topological real projective plane.

(1) General position. A topological circle D ⊂ X is in 'general position' relative to X_1 if it meets X_1 only in points of even order, and crosses X_1 transversally at each of them. Even-order points are interior points of edges (order 2) and even vertices. So D may pass through an even vertex of order 2k. Transversality there means each local straight-through branch has one half on each side of D. This is exactly how a new pseudoline passes through a multiple point of an arrangement.

(2) Relative isotopy. Two such circles D, D' are in the 'same relative position' (isotopic) if one can deform D into D' through circles D_t that stay in general position, while D_t ∩ S stays constant. Here S is the vertex set (written S(K)), so the vertices D passes through are held fixed. Grothendieck lets Φ(D) be the set of facets (open cells: vertices, edges, faces) of (X, X_1) that D meets. He claims Φ(D) = Φ(D') suffices. As a necessary consequence, there is a path f_t (0 ≤ t ≤ 1) of automorphisms of (X, X_1) with f_0 = id and f_1(D) = D'.

(3) Sweeps and specialization. As for pseudoline systems, he defines a 'sweep' (balayage) of D across an even vertex of X_1. He also defines a 'specialization' of D onto a vertex (D moved to pass through the vertex), and conversely 'generizations' that push D off a vertex to one side or the other.
- For fixed D, these specializations and generizations are organized as 'transitions'.
- They lead to a set D̃ attached to D, which forms a family of pairwise disjoint sets (or arcs).
- The drawing shows a green curve D crossing red lines. Thick black segments mark the portions of D between crossings that can be swept. At the left there is a dashed circle at a multiple point that D passes through, with two marks for its two generizations.
- He then announces a notion of 'parallel transport' along D̃. It uses D̃'s natural topological, or better combinatorial, structure and works through specializations and generizations. The sentence breaks off.

Purpose. The previous pages study the moduli or covering space of pseudoline configurations (a D_{2n}-covering, its connectedness, crossing 'superdegenerate' positions). This page sets up the local machinery for adding or moving one curve D relative to a fixed arrangement-like complex. In oriented-matroid terms, this is the stratified space of single-element extensions together with its moves.
errors: The definition of general position is garbled in the manuscript (crossings-out). The intended condition is presumably 'D meets X_1 only at points of even order, transversally'. As written ('s'il rencontre X_1') it reads as merely requiring D to meet X_1.

'Transversal' at a vertex of order 2k is not defined for a general graph. One needs the straight-through pairing of half-edges at the vertex, which exists canonically in the pseudoline case but not in general.

ideas.what: Generalizing pseudoline arrangements to a compact surface with a cellularly embedded graph whose vertices all have even order. Following edges straight through each vertex then gives a system of closed curves on a surface.
ideas.modern_name: Eulerian maps / arrangements of curves on surfaces (generalized pseudoline arrangements)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956) and Grünbaum (1972) for pseudoline arrangements; curve arrangements on surfaces in later topological graph theory
ideas.where_published: Pseudoline systems are only alluded to in Grothendieck's later writings, as far as I know; no published treatment

ideas.what: Circles in general position relative to X_1, allowed to pass transversally through even vertices; isotopy keeping the set of vertices met constant; the set of facets met, Φ(D), as a combinatorial invariant.
ideas.modern_name: Single-element extension of an arrangement and its covector/cocircuit signature (localization)

ideas.what: Sweep of a curve across an even vertex; specialization onto a vertex and generization away from it, forming a poset of positions of D.
ideas.modern_name: Mutations (triangle flips) and the face poset of the extension space
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956) for flips; Sturmfels–Ziegler (1993) for extension spaces

ideas.what: A set D̃ attached to D (apparently its zone or set of sweepable portions), with a 'parallel transport' along it defined combinatorially through specializations and generizations.
ideas.modern_name: Zone of a pseudoline; transport or monodromy along strata of the extension space (closest: connectivity and monodromy of extension spaces)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Zone theorem: Edelsbrunner–Seidel–Sharir; extension-space connectivity: Sturmfels–Ziegler (1993), Mnëv–Richter-Gebert (1993)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sketches a 'parallel transport' along the stratified neighbourhood D̃ of a curve. It runs through specializations and generizations at even vertices, and is set up for arbitrary cellular surfaces with even vertices, not just projective-plane pseudoline arrangements. The sentence breaks off and the next page is only a drawing. The literature studies extension spaces mainly for oriented matroids, i.e. pseudoline/pseudosphere arrangements, and asks about connectivity rather than a transport or monodromy structure. A transport structure on generic-curve positions relative to an Eulerian map on a surface of arbitrary genus does not seem to be a developed topic.
missed.quote: Il y a une notion de transport parallèle par D̃, munie de sa structure top naturelle (ou plutôt par sa structure combinatoire) par spécialisations et générisations
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It suggests treating extension spaces (whose connectivity can fail, by Mnëv–Richter-Gebert) as carrying monodromy or local-system data. It also extends extension-space theory beyond oriented matroids to curve arrangements on surfaces. Both are modest but open-ended directions.

missed.claim: This page and its neighbours tie the moduli or covering space of pseudoline configurations (the D_{2n}-covering on the previous page) to a stratified, specialization/generization picture of positions of one curve. Grothendieck uses his algebraic-geometric vocabulary here (specialization and generization as for points of a scheme, 'facettes'). The page thus implicitly reads the extension poset as a finite topological space or stratified site. This reading is not standard in oriented-matroid theory.
missed.quote: les sp. et spéc. et des générisations à partir de D
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It fits the later view of oriented-matroid realization and extension spaces as stratified spaces (MacPhersonians, combinatorial Grassmannians), a view credited to others in the 1990s.

deep.surprise_reason: The material is mostly a natural, routine generalization of the pseudoline machinery from previous pages. Its counterparts (single-element extensions, flips, zones, extension spaces) are well known and credited to Las Vergnas, Ringel, and Sturmfels–Ziegler. Mildly notable: the move to arbitrary cellular surfaces with even vertices, the scheme-theoretic specialization/generization language, and the unfinished 'parallel transport' idea.
transcription_corrections: 'en position st.' should read 'en position générale' (the term defined earlier on the page).

The general-position condition likely reads 's'il ne rencontre X_1 qu'en des points ...' or similar; the transcribed 's'il rencontre X_1' loses the restriction (the image has a struck-out word before 'rencontre').
'S(K)' is probably the vertex set ('sommets') of the cellular complex; its argument is hard to read in the image.
'... famille d'ens ... deux à deux disjoints': there is an insertion above the line, possibly 'ouverts'/'d'arcs ouverts'; the reading is uncertain.
Margin note '87' is the archive page number.
